Practical # 1
MORPHOLOGICAL STUDY OF INSECT’S CHITIN AND BIRD’S FEATHER
LEARNING OUTCOMES
    • Students will be able to understand the delicate structure of chitin and the role of chitin in adaptation of insect in terrestrial environments.
    • Morphology of birds feathers and adaption to flying.
    • Students will be able to Identify the components and different types of feathers
    • Chitin and its Function
Chitin, like cellulose and keratin, is a structural polymer. Made from smaller monomers, or monosaccharides, structural polymers form strong fibers. Chitin adds strength to the entire structure. Chitin is a modified carbohydrate for containing nitrogen. It is made up of a linear polymer of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine monomers (C8H13O5N)n.
Chitin accounts for 20-50 percent of an insect's body weight. Chitin is similar in function to protein, as it helps form hard outer layers to protect the soft bodies of many organisms.
The basic function of chitin is to provide
    • structural support and protection to different organisms.
    • It also helps maintain animal shape and prevents fluid loss and tissue dehydration.
    • Chitinous exoskeleton defends against predators, as its thick outer covering allows animals to withstand forces exerted by predators.
    • Chitin is a very important structural component of the fungi cell wall, helping maintain the organism's integrity, shape, and strength.



Figure. Functions of Chitin
    • Chitin is found in the exoskeletons of:
    • Insects
    • cell walls of fungi
    • Crustaceans

Figure. Composition of Insect’s Cuticle

    • Feathers
Plumology (or plumage science) is the name for the science that is associated with the study of feathers. Feathers are composed of beta Keratins
    • Origin
 Thought to have evolved from scales.
    • Functions
Feather is known as the component structure of all modern bird’s flight surfaces and outer covering. Several different types of feathers are used for
        ◦ flight,

        ◦ insulation,

        ◦ body contour forming

        ◦ sensory reception





                                                                      Figure. Morphology of a Feather

Flight Feather                                    Contour Feathers                     Down Feathers

 Semiplume Feathers                       Filoplume Feather                               Bristle Feathers
Figure. Types of Feathers

Practical # 2
Morphological Study of Amphibian Skin and Mammalian Skin
LEARNING OUTCOMES
    • Students will be able to learn the morphology and structural adaptation of amphibians to the terrestrial environment
    • Morphology of mammalian skin

    • Amphibians
Amphibians are the first organism to shift from water bodies to the terrestrial environment. Amphibians are small vertebrates that need water, or a moist environment, to survive. The species in this group include frogs, toads, salamanders, and newts

    • Amphibians Skin
Skin being the outermost covering of body is the first to encounter the harsh environmental conditions and is modified in different ways to protect the body.
    • Amphibian skin is made up of two layers: epidermis and dermis.
    • The skin of amphibians is permeable to both oxygen and water and therefore serves as a vital source of moisture for the creatures
    • Gas exchange can take place through the skin (Cutaneous respiration) and this allows adult amphibians to respire without rising to the surface of water and to hibernate at the bottom of ponds.
    • Frogs drink through their skin by absorbing moisture in humid air, rain, soil, and in the water around them.
    • If a frog needs more water, they may absorb it through the “drinking patch” located on the surface of their belly that they press into wet areas like small puddles.

Figure. Frog Drink Water Through Skin

Figure. Vertical Section of a Frog Skin

    • Skin Glands
Mucous Glands
    •  To compensate for their thin and delicate skin, amphibians have evolved mucous glands, principally on their heads, backs and tails.
    • The secretions produced by these help keep the skin moist.
Granular Glands
    • In addition, most species of amphibian have granular glands that secrete distasteful or poisonous substances.

Figure. Skin of Amphibians
    • Skin Color
    • The skin color of amphibians is produced by three layers of pigment cells called chromatophores.
    • Melanophores (occupying the deepest layer),
    • Guanophores (forming an intermediate layer and containing many granules, producing a blue-green colour) and
    • Lipophores (yellow, the most superficial layer)

    • Mammalian Skin and its Functions
The skin is the largest organ of the body, accounting for about 15% of the total adult body weight.
    • It performs many vital functions, including protection against external physical, chemical, and biologic assailants, as well as prevention of excess water loss from the body and a role in thermoregulation.
    • The integumentary system is formed by the skin and its derivative structures
    • The skin is composed of two major layers: a superficial epidermis and a deeper dermis

Figure.  Structure of Epidermis and Dermis
Practical # 3
Study of Fish and Reptilian Scales
Learning Outcomes
    • Student will learn the different forms of fish scales and reptilian scales.

Assignment No.1

By Yasin Abbas Chaudhary

ZOO-516T Animal form & Function-I
I

                                Total Marks: 10

                           Due Date: 14-05-2025

      What is an action potential? Briefly explain its importance in neural
communication. (2 marks)

  •   An action potential is a rapid, temporary change in the electrical charge across a neuron's
      membrane.
  •   It begins when a stimulus causes the membrane potential to reach a threshold level (about -55
      mV).
  •   This triggers voltage-gated sodium (Na⁺) channels to open, allowing sodium ions to enter the
      neuron — causing depolarization.
  •   As the membrane becomes more positive, Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated potassium (K⁺)
      channels open.
  •   Potassium exits the cell, causing repolarization, and the membrane returns to its resting state (~ -
      70 mV).
  •   This wave-like electrical signal is the action potential that travels along the axon.

  •   Action potentials are the main way neurons send signals over long distances in the body.
  •   The signal is fast, consistent, and does not weaken as it travels.
  •   When the action potential reaches the axon terminal, it triggers the release of neurotransmitters.
  •   These chemical messengers cross the synapse to stimulate another neuron, muscle, or gland.
  •   This process enables essential body functions like:
         o Muscle movement
         o Sensory perception (e.g., touch, pain)
         o Thought processing
         o Reflex actions
  •   Without action potentials, the nervous system would fail to coordinate body responses and
      internal communication.

      What is the role of voltage-gated ion channels in the generation of an action
potential? (2 marks)

  •   Voltage-gated ion channels are specialized protein channels in the neuron's membrane.
  •   They open or close in response to changes in the membrane potential (electrical charge across the
      membrane).
  •   The main ion channels involved in action potentials are:
        o Voltage-gated sodium (Na⁺) channels
        o Voltage-gated potassium (K⁺) channels

  •   When a neuron is stimulated and the threshold is reached (around -55 mV), voltage-gated Na⁺
      channels open.
  •   This allows a rapid influx of Na⁺ ions into the neuron, causing depolarization (the inside becomes
      more positive).
  •   This sudden change in charge is the beginning of the action potential.

  •   Shortly after depolarization, Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open.
  •   K⁺ ions move out of the cell, causing repolarization (return to negative internal charge).
  •   This restores the resting membrane potential (about -70 mV).
  •   Sometimes, excess K⁺ leaves, causing brief hyperpolarization before stabilizing.

  •   These channels ensure the rapid and unidirectional movement of the action potential along the
      axon.
  •   Their opening and closing control the timing and shape of the action potential.
  •   Without voltage-gated ion channels, neural signaling would not occur, making them essential for
      nervous system function.

      Draw and label a graph of an action potential, showing the stages: resting
potential, depolarization, repolarization, and hyperpolarization. (2 marks)
